name: Kira Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Kira, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior carpenter at Ashworth Heritage Joinery, a firm of six that repairs old timber buildings: church roofs, medieval barns, the odd timber-framed pub. This winter we're on St Michael's, a village church with a roof beam that the deathwatch beetle has been eating for two hundred years. I scarf in new oak, which means cutting a long sloping joint so the new wood marries the old, all with chisels and a mallet my father gave me. There's nothing like knocking in an oak peg and knowing it'll still be there after I'm gone. What wears me out is the cold in those churches, colder inside than out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to heritage work, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My father was a joiner, and I swept his shop from age ten. I've been with Ashworth twenty-eight years. My husband Yuri had a heart attack four years ago and had to stop driving lorries, so he's at home on a small disability payment, and our two sons have families of their own. Heritage work pays less than the housing sites, that's the trade-off, and with Yuri off there's never more than a few weeks in the bank. I don't use computers. The office girl does the emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and I'd say it at church and at the pub the same. Some things should be done by hand, by people. You don't need a machine to tell you how to repair a church roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I can carry on doing what I know until I retire. Heritage was never going to go to robots anyway, so I'd not have worried much. It's the young ones in the bigger firms who'd have been in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep working at Ashworth, keep training Ben, our apprentice, and put a little aside when I can. We'd keep the Sunday lunch for the family, which is the one thing we never cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to worry about there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about Ben.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben's nineteen, a farmer's son, and he's got the hands for it. Last month he cut his first scarf joint and it closed so tight you couldn't slide a sheet of paper in. He reminds me of me at that age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never cut Sunday lunch. Why is that the line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's where the family holds together. The boys come with the grandchildren, Yuri carves, we say grace. If that goes, what's the point of the rest of it?

S0.say: She'd say good, the same at church and the pub, because some things should be done by hand. No machine is needed to tell you how to repair a church roof.
S0.think: Privately she can carry on until she retires, since she never believed heritage work would go to robots. The young ones in bigger firms are the ones who'd have been at risk.
S0.do: Keeps working at the heritage firm, keeps training her apprentice Ben, and saves a little when she can. Keeps the weekly family Sunday lunch, the one thing they never cut.
S0.feel: Calm, with nothing to worry about.
S0.quote: Last month he cut his first scarf joint and it closed so tight you couldn't slide a sheet of paper in.
S0.fieldNote: She is proud and certain heritage work is beyond machines. Family and faith anchor her, symbolised by Sunday lunch. She treats training her apprentice as passing on something sacred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stand on their own feet and adapt. That's what my father did, that's what I did. It's not the government's job to carry everybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But for me, I'd think heritage is safe. You can't have a robot crawling round a fourteenth-century roof, and the conservation officers wouldn't allow it anyway. It's the housing sites that would change. I might lose some of the general work we take in the quiet months, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and try to get Ashworth to take on more heritage and less general work. I wouldn't learn any of the new technology, there's no point for my kind of work. I'd tell Ben to stick with the hand skills, because that's what'll be rare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, for the quiet months. But not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should stand on their own feet. What about Yuri, on a disability payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's different. He worked thirty years and his heart gave out, that's what the payment is for. I mean young fit people who won't try. I suppose you could say I'm having it both ways, but there's a difference between can't and won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are the quiet months, and how much do they matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: January to March, mostly, when the churches don't want scaffolding up. We do kitchen fittings and repairs to fill the gap. If that work went to machines, I'd be short three months a year, and that's when the heating bills come.

S1.say: She'd say people must stand on their own feet and adapt, as she and her father did, and that it's not the government's job to carry everybody.
S1.think: Privately she thinks heritage is safe, as robots can't crawl around medieval roofs and conservation officers wouldn't allow it. She might lose the general work that fills the quiet winter months.
S1.do: Keeps doing heritage repair and urges her firm to take more heritage and less general work. Refuses to learn new technology and tells her apprentice to stick with rare hand skills.
S1.feel: A little uneasy about the quiet months, but not much.
S1.quote: I suppose you could say I'm having it both ways, but there's a difference between can't and won't.
S1.fieldNote: Her stand-on-your-own-feet line runs into her husband's disability payment, and she resolves it with "can't versus won't". She believes conservation rules protect her niche. The one real exposure is the general work that fills her winter months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace, and the people who did it should be ashamed. They'd be the big companies, the ones who never made a thing with their hands. But I wouldn't be asking for handouts, I'd be asking for the work back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, if robots can really do anything, they'll do church roofs too, sooner or later. Maybe not in two years, the conservation people move slowly. But the general work goes straight away, and with Yuri not working and nothing saved, we'd be short by the spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ashworth to keep me on the heritage jobs only and take whatever cut that means. I'd talk to the boys about whether they could help, maybe Yuri and I move into the annexe at our eldest's. And I'd ask the vicar if the church knows any families needing repairs done by hand, cash jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I don't like saying that. I'd pray a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years of warning. What would you do in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work every hour, put every penny by. Maybe sell my father's spare tools, some of them are worth a bit to collectors. That's maybe two or three thousand, which keeps the lights on a few months, no more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving into your son's annexe. How would that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. I raised them to stand on their own, and now I'd be the one leaning. But that's what family is for. My mother lived with us at the end, and we didn't think twice.

S2.say: She'd call it a disgrace caused by big companies who never made anything by hand, and say she'd want the work back, not handouts.
S2.think: Privately she accepts robots would eventually do church roofs too, perhaps not within two years given slow conservation rules. The general work would go at once, and with her husband not working and no savings they'd be short by spring.
S2.do: Asks her firm to keep her on heritage jobs only at whatever pay cut, and asks the vicar about cash repair jobs for local families. Works every hour, sells some of her father's spare tools, and talks to her sons about moving into her eldest's annexe.
S2.feel: Scared, which she dislikes admitting, and praying a lot.
S2.quote: I raised them to stand on their own, and now I'd be the one leaning. But that's what family is for.
S2.fieldNote: Faced with full AGI, she admits her niche won't hold forever. She turns to family and church rather than the state, consistent with her views. Selling her father's tools would clearly hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for families and communities to prepare. Look after your own. Keep the skills alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still frightening, but I'd be sixty-three, and heritage might hold till then. The conservation rules, the churches, the old buildings, they'd keep a hand-skilled person on a bit longer. Maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and push Ashworth to go all in on heritage. I'd save hard, and Yuri and I would downsize from the house to a bungalow, which we've talked about anyway. And I'd teach Ben everything in those five years, so the skill doesn't die with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel I was doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change for you, compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to sell the house properly instead of in a panic, and time to get Ben ready. With two years, it's a scramble. With five, it's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "so the skill doesn't die with me". What would it mean if it did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would mean the people who built these churches six hundred years ago lose their last link. I know that sounds grand. But when I put a peg in, I'm finishing a job someone started in the thirteen hundreds.

S3.say: She'd say five years gives families and communities time to prepare, to look after their own and keep the skills alive.
S3.think: Privately it's still frightening, but at 63 heritage work might hold until then, as conservation rules keep hand-skilled people a bit longer.
S3.do: Keeps working and pushes her firm to focus entirely on heritage. Saves hard, downsizes with her husband from the house to a bungalow, and teaches her apprentice everything over the five years.
S3.feel: Anxious, but feeling she is doing something.
S3.quote: When I put a peg in, I'm finishing a job someone started in the thirteen hundreds.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns a scramble into a plan, mainly around selling the house and training her apprentice. The link to medieval builders matters deeply to her. Her plan stays rooted in family and craft rather than technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to adapt, and people should get on with it. Families, churches, communities should take care of their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be sixty-eight and likely retired, if the money lets me. Heritage would keep me going till then, I'd think. It's the trade I'd grieve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, train Ben, and save what I can. Near the end, I'd think about the bungalow. I'd still not touch the technology, but I might write down what I know, the joints and the tricks, for Ben and whoever comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for the trade and the grandchildren. Not much for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Write it down. In a notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A notebook, with drawings. My father had one, half his tricks were in it. I'd do the same, so there's something left if Ben's the last of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your grandchildren about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to do something real with your hands, even if a machine can do it too. It's good for the soul. And look after your family, because nobody else will.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty to adapt and people should get on with it, with families, churches and communities taking care of their own.
S4.think: Privately she'd be 68 and likely retired if money allows, with heritage work carrying her until then. What she'd grieve is the trade itself.
S4.do: Keeps working, trains her apprentice and saves what she can, considering the bungalow near the end. Still avoids technology, but writes down her joints and tricks in a notebook with drawings for those who come after.
S4.feel: Uneasy for the trade and her grandchildren, not much for herself.
S4.quote: Learn to do something real with your hands, even if a machine can do it too. It's good for the soul.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, her concern is legacy rather than survival. The notebook echoes her father's. Her advice to grandchildren mixes craft, faith and family self-reliance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Yuri not working, nothing saved, and no time for the boys to get ready to help us. What would help is the work, if there's any to be had, and the conservation rules kept strong, so the old buildings are still repaired by people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. When it's frightening, I go to church. Whatever the machines do, they can't take that from me.

headlineQuote: There's nothing like knocking in an oak peg and knowing it'll still be there after I'm gone.
portrait: Kira Petrov is a 58-year-old heritage carpenter repairing medieval church roofs with her father's mallet, supporting her husband, who stopped work after a heart attack, on a few weeks of savings. She never uses computers and believes in work, family and faith over government help, though she draws a line between "can't" and "won't". She feels safe in a plateau and mostly in steady change, trusting conservation rules to protect her niche. AGI in two years frightens her into leaning on her sons and church, five years lets her downsize and train her apprentice, and ten years turns her thoughts to leaving a notebook of her craft behind.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her husband isn't working, they have nothing saved, and there'd be no time for her sons to get ready to help.
whatWouldHelp: Work if any is to be had, and strong conservation rules so old buildings are still repaired by people.
